title: 2025 year-end finances and reserve policy changes
subtitle: Building permit audit found no bottleneck; at-home accessible voting for 2030; committee for election compliance.
overview: The committee of the whole reviewed the City's 2025 year-end financial reports. It recommended how to cover or allocate operating deficits and surpluses, approved capital budget adjustments, and backed an updated Development Charge Exemptions Policy. That policy creates separate reserve funds so that tax- and rate-funded exemption costs are tracked apart from developer-paid charges. All three recommendations went to Council {{vote:m4}} {{vote:m5}} {{vote:m6}}.

The committee also received the internal audit of building permits and inspections for information {{vote:m3}}. The audit found permitting is not holding up housing, and it pointed to complaint tracking and regular performance reporting as areas to improve. Separately, the committee recommended directing the City Clerk to prioritize voting methods that let voters independently mark a ballot at home in the 2030 election {{vote:m7}}.

The committee also adopted a consent item on a joint election compliance audit committee. Before the open session, it met in closed session on parkland acquisitions and an expression of interest for 170 Stephanie Drive. The Mayor reported only that direction was given to staff on both items.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended allocating the 2025 tax-supported and non-tax-supported results to or from specific reserves, and adding $175,000 to the 2026 operating budget for an HR job evaluation system funded from the Strategic Initiatives Reserve.
The committee recommended approving the 2025 and 2026 capital budget adjustments, which net to an increase of $1,732,242 in the 2026 capital budget.

decisions.item: Reserves, debt and development charge exemptions
decisions.detail: The committee received the 2025 long-term financial statement, and recommended approving the updated Development Charge Exemptions Policy, creating DC Exemption reserve funds, and moving $2,000,000 from the Accumulated Sick Leave (Fire) reserve to the WSIB reserve in 2026.
The committee received the audit report on building permit approvals and inspections for information.
The committee recommended directing the City Clerk to prioritize voting methods that let voters independently mark a ballot at home, and to report back in 2028.
The committee adopted a consent report on the 2026–2030 joint municipal election compliance audit committee, including delegating member appointments and terms-of-reference updates to the City Clerk.

debate: On the building audit, councillors welcomed findings that permit timelines are being met. One councillor asked about differences in basement-unit fees compared with other municipalities, and staff said a building permit fee review coming to Council in June would answer that.

Another councillor asked whether the fee study could ease the forecast 2026 building services deficit. Staff said the study aims to improve cost recovery and reduce reliance on large projects, but would not predict 2026 results because they depend on which applications come forward.

On complaint tracking, staff said a citywide approach would come with a future customer relationship management system, which is in the 2028 IT capital forecast. Departments use their own tracking in the meantime.

A delegate spoke on the capital budget, raising questions about the cost and evaluation of the Speedvale Avenue and pedestrian bridge projects. Staff replied that capital budgets are public and managed through the City's budget process, and said they would provide final project accounting on request.

Councillors asked whether the debt ratio crossing a risk threshold is a concern for the credit rating. Staff said it is one factor among many, that the rating could be affected, and that debt servicing remains well under the legislated limit.

On the voting methods motion, one councillor asked what "prioritize" meant. The mover said it fills an accessibility gap for voters who cannot use paper or mail ballots without help, and does not rank at-home voting above voting centres. Staff said the direction fits work already planned.
